implementation_notes: Thread::ConditionVariable is the classic wait set: wait(mutex) must be called while holding the mutex, releases it and parks the thread, and re-acquires before returning, while signal wakes one waiter and broadcast all of them; MonitorMixin adds a monitor object with condition helpers, and Thread::Queue implements the item/space guard directly. Ruby's threads are OS threads, so the wait is a real park, and the predicate loop is mandatory because a wait can return for reasons other than the predicate becoming true. Use the condition variable when the guard is not queue-shaped and Queue/SizedQueue when it is.
code_sketch:
mutex, cv, queue = Mutex.new, ConditionVariable.new, []

def take(mutex, cv, queue)
  mutex.synchronize do
    cv.wait(mutex) while queue.empty?   # release + park, re-check predicate
    queue.shift
  end
end

def put(mutex, cv, queue, item)
  mutex.synchronize { queue.push(item); cv.broadcast }   # change, then notify
end
pitfalls: ConditionVariable#wait raises ThreadError unless the mutex is held by the calling thread, so the wait must sit inside synchronize.
In the default (non-Ractor) runtime the GVL does not protect your invariants: all guarded state must still be read and written under the mutex.
A signal with no waiting thread is lost, so the predicate must be updated before signalling.

variants.name: Thread::Queue / SizedQueue blocking pop
variants.implementation_notes: Thread::Queue is the library realization: pop (aliases deq, shift) blocks until an element is available, push on a SizedQueue blocks while it is full, and close releases waiting consumers with nil - guarded suspension with the queue itself as the guard, no explicit condition variable needed. Prefer it for the 'an item is available' guard and keep the condition-variable form for predicates that are not queue-shaped.
variants.code_sketch:
q = Thread::Queue.new

consumer = Thread.new do
  while (item = q.pop)      # blocks while empty, returns nil after close
    handle(item)
  end
end

q.push(task)                # wakes exactly one waiting consumer
q.close                     # release the consumer once everything is sent
pitfalls: pop blocks forever on an empty open queue, so shutdown must close the queue or push a sentinel.
close makes pop return nil, which is indistinguishable from a nil element: never enqueue nil when close is used for termination.
